name: 日本酒とおばんざい 新奈 (Nihonshu to Obanzai Niina)

claims.text: The menu is home-style obanzai blending Japanese, Western and Chinese cooking, which typically involves soy sauce and miso (wheat-containing) and dishes such as pasta salad; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Omakase courses regularly include fish, meat and seasonal game and generally rely on Japanese dashi, so vegan separation is not assured; requirements would need to be arranged in advance.

With only eight counter seats and a single proprietress who chooses the courses and discusses each guest's preferences directly, there is room to talk through dietary needs in advance via Instagram, though no formal allergy program is documented.

Travel coverage states that vegetarian and vegan guests can be accommodated for the tea-rice set, indicating the kitchen is willing to adjust, but no formal allergy/cross-contact protocol is published.
The core meal is a simple, rice-and-vegetable homestyle set with miso soup and Nara pickles, and the egg is an optional add-on, making it easy to keep the plate plant-based on request.

name: お台所＆サロン かたつむり (Odaidokoro & Salon Katatsumuri)

claims.text: The kitchen prepares everything by hand and already uses eggless vegan mayonnaise in at least one salad, suggesting some willingness to accommodate plant-based eaters if asked in advance.
Courses include wheat-based items such as Miwa sōmen noodles and soy-seasoned dishes, with no documented gluten-free protocol.
Cuisine uses Japanese soy sauce and a dashi base typical of kaiseki, both of which involve wheat and fish; no gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The dashi is made from katsuobushi (bonito) and kombu and the menu features Yamato beef, so vegan diners cannot rely on the standard courses.

name: 御菓子処 優月 (Okashidokoro Yuzuki)

claims.text: Wheat-flour confections (dorayaki-style sweets, manju, baked goods) are made in the same back-of-shop workshop as rice- and bean-based sweets, so cross-contamination with wheat is likely.

name: おむすび処 和が家 (Omusubi-dokoro Wagaya)

claims.text: The owner is selective about ingredients, choosing a specific Hokkaido rice variety along with particular salt and miso, and works alone, so it is feasible to ask directly about how a dish is made.
Skewers are basted in a house tare (sweet soy-based sauce), which is standard wheat-containing soy sauce; dishes such as ponzu-dressed items and fried chicken also rely on soy sauce and wheat batter.
The kitchen is dedicated to chicken and egg dishes grilled on a shared charcoal grill, so there is no separation for plant-based diners.

name: お庭 シェイブアイス ミラコロ (Oniwa Shaveice Miracolo)

claims.text: Syrups are made in-house from fruit and sugar, and the core product is shaved ice rather than wheat- or batter-based, so several bowls may suit avoiders of gluten if toppings are checked.
